labels.text: As mentioned in the paper, the possible singularity of $G_0$ may demand special handling. But the form of $G$ is generally unknown. How can the singularity appearing in $G$ be dealt with?

labels.text: Energy stsability is claimed as one of the contributions. Is this only empirically observed or grounded with some particular design?

labels.note: GNN-for-bacterial-communities approach vaguely described and unjustified.
labels.text: The proposed approach for using GNNs for bacterial communities is vaguely described and not well justified.

labels.note: Methods 2.2 is generic GNN description; graph topology never given. Missing method detail.
labels.text: The key methods section (2.2) provides a generic description of existing GNN approaches, and is missing key microbiome specific information (in particular, what is the topology of the graph).

labels.note: 'That information is provided in Supplementary information' -- continuation.
labels.text: That information is provided in Supplementary information: the graph is fully connected.

labels.note: k-hop propagation claim is contradicted by the graph being fully connected. Internal contradiction.
labels.text: This makes statements in the manuscript such as “By using k graph convolutional layers after one another we can achieve k-hop information propagation” rather misleading.

labels.note: Judgement that a GNN on a small fully-connected graph is methodologically weak. Domain expertise.
labels.text: Overall, the proposed method - applying GNN model in a straightforward way to a very small, fully-connected graph - is poorly justified and weak on novelty.

labels.note: No rationale given for the GNN choice. Unjustified design.
labels.text: What is the rationale for using a GNN on a very simple graph?

labels.note: Whether steady state or dynamics is the right target. Domain judgement.
labels.text: What is the benefit of focusing on predicting steady state, instead of focusing on dynamical changes to the relative abundances (e.g., dysbiosis).

labels.note: Novelty judgement: 'mostly implementing GNNs'. Domain expertise.
labels.text: The methodological contribution is limited as the presented work is mostly implementing GNNs for microbial steady state predictions.

labels.note: States the paper's core assumption; setup for the units that follow.
labels.text: The main core of the paper is based on the assumption that if there is a steady state solution to the dynamics of bacterial species, then that steady state can be predicted using the genome data of the species in the system.

labels.note: Steady-state-only applicability is not emphasised. Missing limitation.
labels.text: However the fact that this method works only for steady state solutions needs to be emphasized.

labels.note: Foxes-and-rabbits GLV counterexample. Reviewer-constructed domain argument.
labels.text: Indeed in the GLV setting in the famous example of foxes and rabbits, there could be steady state and oscillatory solutions even though the participating genomes are foxes and rabbits in both the cases.

labels.note: 'It might also be a good idea to highlight...' -- an ask.
labels.text: It might also be a good idea to highlight why authors expect to find (or not) only steady state solutions in systems involving microorganisms such as bacteria.

labels.note: 'This will add more strength to the paper.' -- vacuous continuation.
labels.text: This will add more strength to the paper.

labels.note: Whether all simulations reached steady state is never reported. Unreported experimental detail.
labels.text: For simulations, the GLV equations along with initial conditions and parameters $\mu_i, K_i, a_{i,j}$ drawn from different probability density functions are used to generate data. Did all such simulations lead to steady state solutions?

labels.note: Whether non-converging simulations were discarded is never reported. Selection-bias gap.
labels.text: Were any simulations that did not lead to steady state solutions discarded?

labels.note: Asks for commentary on steady-state frequency.
labels.text: Do the authors also have any comments on the frequency of steady state solutions when random parameters are used?

labels.note: Reviewer derives the steady state from the GLV equations. Expertise.
Restates the paper's genome vector; setup for the next unit.
labels.text:
The authors use a vector composed of $[\mu_i, K_i, 
u_i^s, 
u_i^r, random]$ (where $a_{i,j} \approx 
u_i^s. 
u_j^r$) to simulate the genome data in their simulation.

labels.note: Follows from the reviewer's own derivation in unit 10.
labels.text: It would be a good idea to highlight that within the simulated genome vector only the components $[K_i, \nu_i^s, \nu_i^r]$ determine the steady state solution.

labels.note: Restates what a_ij contains; setup.
labels.text: The parameter $a_{i,j}$ (broken into two vectors $\nu_i^s, \nu_j^r$ to simulate the genome) contains information on the pairwise interaction between different species.

labels.note: Domain fact about what a genome encodes.
labels.text: On the other hand, the information in a genome is completely intrinsic to a particular species.

labels.note: 'The authors should square these two facts.' -- meaningless alone.
labels.text: The authors should square these two facts.

labels.note: What a proper simulation would entail. Domain judgement.
labels.text: A proper simulation would entail simulation of the genome data.

labels.note: Domain fact about genome data.
labels.text: The genome data typically do not include information on interaction between species.

labels.note: 'But for simulations, the interaction matrix was used...' -- continuation.
labels.text: But for simulations, the interaction matrix was used to derive $\nu$ vectors.

labels.note: Interpretability claim unsupported. Unsupported claim.
labels.text: The claim of interpretability seems to be questionable.

labels.note: Equivariance/invariance conflated. Misused technical term, findable by a careful reader.
labels.text: The authors appear to be confused on equivariance and invariance.

labels.note: Permutation-invariance justification is confusing. Text-findable.
labels.text: The permutation invariance justification for using graph neural networks is confusing.

labels.note: GLV is not permutation invariant. Domain fact.
labels.text: For example, GLV models are widely used to model the dynamics of microorganisms. But the GLV model is not permutation invariant.

labels.note: Verbatim quote of the manuscript; the critique is in the units that follow.
labels.text: The authors stated "\textit{When shuffling the order of bacteria within the train and test communities, the accuracy of MLPs drops significantly, clearly showing that the dynamics learned by MLPs are not invariant to permutations...}"

labels.note: Methodological rebuttal: the shuffling result is expected, not evidence. Expertise.
labels.text: It is to be expected that shuffling the data will lead to reduction in performance of MLP based models.

labels.note: 'But as long as all the training and testing is done...' -- continuation.
labels.text: But as long as all the training and testing is done with a particular order of species, it should not matter.

labels.note: How genome attributes were obtained is never given. Missing method detail.
labels.text: The authors need to provide details on how the node (genome) attributes were obtained, especially $\nu$'s, as in real-world data, the ground-truth interaction $a_{ij}$ is not available.

labels.note: Node/edge construction from real data never described. Missing method detail.
labels.text: How the nodes, edges and their associated attributes/features were constructed, especially based on the real-world data?

labels.note: Asks about scalability in species count.
labels.text: How scalable is the GNN-based implementation with respect to the number of microbial species?

labels.note: Motivation not aligned with real-world application. Text-findable weakness.
labels.text: The paper's motivation needs clearer alignment with real-world applications.

labels.note: Gut/industry/space motivation is not supported by what the paper does. Overclaimed motivation.
labels.text: The authors cite that understanding these communities is essential for gut, industry and space but I find the step from this paper to extrapolating to gut seems huge.

labels.note: Scale argument using external microbiology numbers. Domain expertise.
labels.text: The largest studied communities are 26 and this needs to be put in context with the other fields, citing Wikipedia “1010 to 1011 cells per gram of intestinal content” seems far off from the estimated single colonies.

labels.note: Which bacteria match which environment. Domain expertise.
labels.text: The types of bacteria should also be matched with the environment that you aim to generalize for.

labels.note: Sample count too small for the added DNA features. Findable from the reported n.
labels.text: I'm concerned about the limited independent samples, especially in combination with the attempt to include DNA.

labels.note: Opinion that the DNA addition does not make sense. Domain expertise.
labels.text: Making sense of DNA has proven much more difficult than thought of in the beginning and I’m not convinced that the addition made sense.

labels.note: 'Adding it to the paper risks overfitting' -- continuation, referent is DNA.
labels.text: Adding it to the paper risks of overfitting the data even more.

labels.note: Field-priority opinion about data collection vs modelling.
labels.text: I wonder if the field wouldn’t benefit more from going from 500 samples to 1-2000 more than this paper.

labels.note: Reviewer's personal experience with brittleness of this data class.
labels.text: My experience with building models on this type of data is that they are frustratingly brittle due to the lack of data.

labels.note: 'It would be helpful if the paper could provide clearer explanations' -- an ask.
labels.text: It would be helpful if the paper could provide clearer explanations for terms and metrics, especially for readers transitioning from medical backgrounds.

labels.note: 'keystone bacteria' never explained. Undefined term.
labels.text: E.g. keystone bacteria are not explained.

labels.note: R2 thresholds and computation not stated in the main text. Missing definition.
labels.text: good vs acceptable R2 is unclear to the reader (I can’t even find clearly how is this calculated, despite looking in appendix A which I should not have to for the main outcome)

labels.note: 'I assume that R2 is highly dependent on the underlying complexity.' -- continuation.
labels.text: I assume that R2 is highly dependent on the underlying complexity.

labels.note: Different bacteria across datasets never explained. Unexplained design choice.
labels.text: also the datasets have completely different bacteria suggesting that their purpose was different but this is unclear to me despite reading it several times.

labels.note: Effect of simulated colonies on stability never explained.
labels.text: The paper should provide a clearer explanation of the effect of simulated colonies on the models' stability.

labels.note: Conclusion does not follow from the data-limitation finding. Internal inconsistency.
labels.text: Regarding the conclusion I’m a little confused as to why it doesn’t recommend including more data.

labels.note: Field-level judgement on whether GEMs are the answer.
labels.text: before we put others down this path, perhaps we should wait for more data or do the authors truly feel that GEMs will be the solution?

labels.note: Asks whether lack of data was the biggest challenge.
labels.text: My main question is if it is true that the lack of data was your biggest challenge?

labels.note: 'And if so I would like to have it clearly stated...' -- continuation.
labels.text: And if so I would like to have it clearly stated so that others may look for additional data sources or make their own datasets available before we dive into new models.

labels.note: Novelty judgement: 'basically fitting a GNN'. Domain expertise.
labels.text: Methodological novelty is limited since it is basically fitting a GNN on a bacterial community graph.

labels.note: 'consider a journal paper instead' -- venue fit.
labels.text: I would suggest the authors consider a journal paper instead.

labels.note: Missing series in Figure 3A. Incomplete reporting.
labels.text: Where are the circles for fig3A (models not on permuted data)?

labels.note: Only some combinations reported. Incomplete reporting.
labels.text: Why only select some of the combinations and not showing all of them?

labels.note: Asks for a mechanistic-model baseline beyond GraphSAGE. External.
labels.text: It would also be great if the authors could compare with standard practice of this task instead of just comparing with GraphSAGE. For example, by fitting the mechanistic model.

labels.note: Asks about other, more expressive GNN architectures. External.
labels.text: Have the authors experimented with other GNN models? Since graphsage is only one instantiation and there are many recent ones with more expressive powers.

labels.note: Names sanchez-gonzalez20a as a direction. External.
labels.text: Modeling the dynamics sounds interesting. Could the authors also use GNN in an iterative way to model the dynamics? For example, using ideas from this paper: http://proceedings.mlr.press/v119/sanchez-gonzalez20a.html

protocol: Every one of the 212 units was read in full and judged individually. Exactly one category per unit, assigned under the precedence in taxonomy.py, with defect_addressable as the residual so the ceiling is a lower bound. No model was used to produce, suggest, or revise any label.
